title: Raghunatha Bhagavatacharya
html:
A Name Given by the Lord

Among those whom Sri Chaitanya blessed with His mercy on the banks of the Ganga was a brahmana of Varahanagara, learned in the “Srimad-Bhagavatam.” Vrindavana Dasa does not name him: in the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” he is only “a fortunate brahmana” in whose house the Lord stayed. The name by which all Vaishnavas know him — Bhagavatacharya, “the teacher of the ‘Bhagavata’” — was given to him by Mahaprabhu Himself, on hearing him read the “Bhagavatam” full of bhakti-rasa. So he is called by Krishnadasa Kaviraja in the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” and by Kavi Karnapura in the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” — “Srimad Bhagavatacharya.”

His own name, Raghunatha, we know from Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati. In his “Gaudiya-bhashya” on the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” he writes of the verse in which this brahmana appears: “The name of the brahmana indicated by the phrase eka brahmanera ghare (in the house of a brahmana) is Sri Raghunatha Bhagavata Acharya. His description can be found in the commentary ‘Anubhashya’ on the ‘Chaitanya-charitamrita’ [Adi 10.113]” (on CB, Antya 5.110). And the “Anubhashya” itself says: “His name is said to have been ‘Raghunatha.’” The biographies also call him Sri Raghunatha Pandita, Sri Bhagavatacharya and Srila Bhagavatacharya Prabhu.1

Of his family and the years of his life the sources say nothing: we do not know when he was born, nor when and where he left this world; nor are his days found in the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math. We know only that he was a brahmana and lived in Varahanagara.

The Sripat at Varahanagara

Varahanagara (today Baranagar) lies on the Ganga, about three and a half miles north of Calcutta; it is now the northern edge of the great city. There, in the quarter of Malipara, is Bhagavatacharya's sripat.2 Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura writes in the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya” that Bhagavatacharya lived in Varahanagara and that his abode is still called “the pata of Bhagavatacharya.” Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Anubhashya” names the same place: “His pata is at Malipara in Varahanagara (about three and a half miles north of Calcutta), on the bank of the Ganga.”

By the early twentieth century the pata had fallen into disrepair; Srila Bhaktisiddhanta reports that its servitor then was Dhirendra Ganguli, son of the late Rajachandra Ganguli. One of the biographies adds that a manuscript in Bhagavatacharya's own hand — his book, of which more below — is still shown at the sripat.

The Lord Listens to the “Bhagavatam”

This was when Mahaprabhu, already a sannyasi, came from Nilachala to Gauda and went along the Ganga from one village of devotees to the next. After spending some days at Panihati with Raghava Pandita, He came to Varahanagara. Vrindavana Dasa relates:

“Then the Lord came to Varahanagara, to the house of a most fortunate brahmana. That brahmana was thoroughly learned in the ‘Bhagavata’; seeing the Lord, he began to read the ‘Bhagavata.’ Hearing him read of bhakti-yoga, Gaurachandra Narayana was overwhelmed with ecstasy.” (CB, Antya 5.110–112)

On seeing the Lord the brahmana began to read — and that reading was his service to the Lord. And the Lord, who is Himself the subject of the “Bhagavatam,” listened to him in order to glorify the reader and show the world what the “Bhagavatam” read with bhakti is worth:

“‘Read on! Read on!’ cried Sri Gauranga-raya, roaring and thundering again and again. The brahmana read, immersed in the highest bliss, and the Lord danced, forgetful of the external world. Hearing verse after verse on the glory of bhakti, He fell to the ground again and again. Such was the love the Lord revealed, and seeing Him fall, everyone was afraid. In this way, for three praharas of the night, the ocean of virtues danced, listening to the ‘Bhagavata.’” (CB, Antya 5.113–117)

The loss of “external consciousness” here is no swoon and no worldly intoxication: it is prema, which the Lord tastes in the mood of His devotee, and the fear of those around Him is the fear of those who love Him lest He be hurt.

Returning to external consciousness, the Lord joyfully embraced the brahmana (Antya 5.118) and said:

“Never have I heard anyone else read the ‘Bhagavata’ like this. Therefore your name is ‘Bhagavatacharya.’ Do no other work but this.” (CB, Antya 5.119–120)3

Hearing what title the Lord had bestowed on the brahmana, everyone loudly sang “Hari! Hari!” (Antya 5.121). The Lord's praise is not a judgment of “skill,” nor an academic degree: it is mercy toward a service and, with it, a commission. Mahaprabhu named him for his service and told him to know no other work, and Bhagavatacharya gave the rest of his life to the “Bhagavatam” — to reading it, explaining it and rendering it into Bengali. The reader of the “Bhagavatam” whom the Lord acknowledges is one whose reading awakens love of God, not admiration for learning.

A Disciple of Gadadhara Pandita

Bhagavatacharya names Sri Gadadhara Pandita Gosvami as his guru. In the opening verse of blessing of his book he bows to his true guru — Gadadhara, the best of the twice-born, wholly devoted to bhakti, whose form is the form of a servant of his Master; by the Master, as one of the biographies explains, he means Sri Krishna-Chaitanya.4 This does not make Gadadhara a “mere servant”: service to Mahaprabhu is his eternal nature, for Gadadhara is a manifestation of Sri Radha Herself.

Krishnadasa Kaviraja, listing the branches of Gadadhara's tree, places him among the first:

“The finest of them is Dhruvananda; after him come Shridhara Brahmachari, Bhagavatacharya and Haridasa Brahmachari.” (CC, Adi 12.79)5

In the “Charitamrita” he is also named among the branches of the tree of Mahaprabhu Himself, beside Thakura Saranga:

“Ramadasa, Kavidatta, Sri Gopala dasa, Bhagavatacharya, Thakura Saranga dasa.” (CC, Adi 10.113)

A little further on the name is repeated, and it is the same person (Adi 10.119). And in the list of the branches of Sri Advaita Acharya we read:

“Other branches are Bhagavata Acharya, Vishnudasa Acharya, Chakrapani Acharya and Ananta Acharya.” (CC, Adi 12.58)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta comments on this verse: “Bhagavatacharya was at first among Advaita's associates and later joined Gadadhara's associates” (“Anubhashya” on Adi 12.58). So in the “Charitamrita” one and the same Bhagavatacharya is named in three places: he was with Advaita Acharya and afterwards came to Gadadhara.6

The “Krishna-prema-tarangini”

The Lord's commission — “do no other work” — Bhagavatacharya fulfilled as a writer too. His book, the “Sri Krishna-prema-tarangini” (“The River of Love for Krishna”), is a rendering of the “Srimad-Bhagavatam” in Bengali verse. Kavi Karnapura says of him in the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika”: “Srimad Bhagavatacharya, the author of the booklet ‘Krishna-prema-tarangini,’ exceedingly dear to Gauranga” (GGD 203). And Yadunandana Dasa in the “Shakha-nirnayamrita” honors him thus: “I praise Bhagavatacharya, dear to Gauranga, who composed the great book named ‘Prema-tarangini’” (verse 6; cited by Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Anubhashya” on CC, Adi 12.58).

He undertook the book, according to one of the biographies, only after he had received the darshan of Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. It was not written for scholarly fame: the author himself says that, having studied the “Bhagavatam,” he composed it for the joy of those not versed in learning — so that they too might receive the “Bhagavatam” and devotion to Sri Krishna. This is mercy, not simplification.

The first nine cantos of the “Bhagavatam” are set out in it briefly, yet the meaning of each is unfolded so fully and skillfully that the biography calls it the greatest of wonders. In many places the author sings the incomparable glory of Sri Gaurasundara: he glorifies Krishna — the complete Brahman, whose pastimes are wondrous — Jagannatha, who appeared in Nilachala, and Sri Gauranga, the Lord in the form of Chaitanya, who bestows prema-bhakti and gives shelter to His devotees (so in the Tenth Canto, chapter 1, and in the Eleventh, chapter 5).7 A rendering of the “Bhagavatam” made by a disciple of Gadadhara is the “Bhagavatam” read through the eyes of a devotee of Gauranga. The manuscript in the author's own hand is kept, as we have said, at his sripat in Malipara.

Shveta-manjari

In the eternal pastimes of Vraja Bhagavatacharya is Shveta-manjari. Kavi Karnapura in the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” lists twenty-seven maidservants whom Sri Radha has appointed each to her own service, and names those as whom they came into Gaura's pastimes. Shveta-manjari is the eleventh in the list of gopis, and the eleventh in the list of Gaura's associates is “Srimad Bhagavatacharya, the author of the booklet ‘Krishna-prema-tarangini’” (GGD 195, 203). So too Srila Bhaktisiddhanta understands it: “he is Shveta-manjari of Vraja” (“Anubhashya” on CC, Adi 12.58).8

In Later Traditions

Bhagavatacharya's name lives on in the Vaishnava prayers of homage (vandanas). The “Bhakti-ratnakara” of Narahari Chakravarti opens by glorifying the Lord's associates, and among them: “Glory to Bhagavatacharya, Madhava and Shridhara!” (1.34); various “Vaishnava-vandanas” also name him (“Srimat Bhagavatacharya”).

Later books also mention a Bhagavata Acharya at the great festival in Kheturi: the “Prema-vilasa,” the “Bhakti-ratnakara” and the “Narottama-vilasa” name him among the mahantas of Gadadhara Pandita's branch who gathered for the festival — beside Vaninatha Brahmachari, Chaitanya-vallabha Dasa, Pushpa-Gopala and Hari Acharya. Whether this is the same Raghunatha Bhagavatacharya who read the “Bhagavatam” to the Lord, the sources do not say.9

Significance

Almost the whole life of Raghunatha Bhagavatacharya is contained in one night and one word of the Lord. Listening to him, Mahaprabhu danced for three praharas, named him for his service and told him to know no other work — and he knew none: he explained the “Bhagavatam,” rendered it for simple people, and in that rendering glorified Gaura. That is why the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” calls him “exceedingly dear to Gauranga,” and why for Vaishnavas his name sounds like the Lord's commission itself: the true reader of the “Bhagavatam” is one whose reading awakens prema.

Notes

  1. The name “Raghunatha” is not found in the “Chaitanya-bhagavata,” the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” or the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika.” The “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” (200) names “a certain brahmana Raghunatha, who served Gauranga alone” — this is another person (Varangada), not the one of verse 203.
  2. Malipara as the place of the house where the Lord stayed is known from the tradition of the sripat and from the “Anubhashya”; the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” names only Varahanagara.
  3. In the Bengali: iha vina ara kona na kariha karya — “apart from this, do no other work.” Srila Bhaktisiddhanta also cites these verses in the “Anubhashya” on CC, Adi 10.113.
  4. We do not have the text of the “Krishna-prema-tarangini,” and we give the verse only in substance, as one of the biographies cites and explains it; the text printed there contains a misprint, and Gadadhara's epithet differs between the verse and the explanation (“loving bhakti” and “loving the devotees”).
  5. The name “Raghunatha” for this verse comes from the edition's numbered heading; the Bengali text of the verse has only “Bhagavatacharya.”
  6. According to the “Prema-vilasa” and the “Advaita-prakasha,” Bhagavatacharya is Bada Shyamadasa, a pandita-digvijayi: he came to Shantipura to debate with Advaita Acharya, was defeated, took refuge at His feet, received the Krishna mantra and became a great authority on the “Bhagavatam”; the name “Bhagavatacharya” was given him by Advaita Himself (“Advaita-prakasha” 6.76), and, according to these books, it was he who arranged Advaita's marriage. One of the biographies gives this version beside the account of Gadadhara's disciple without reconciling them. The “Chaitanya-bhagavata,” the “Charitamrita” and the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” say nothing of Shyamadasa, and we follow them and the “Anubhashya”: the Bhagavatacharya who received his name from Mahaprabhu was first with Advaita, then with Gadadhara; Srila Bhaktisiddhanta does not mention Shyamadasa here.
  7. These passages we give only in substance, as one of the biographies cites them: we do not have the book itself.
  8. The correspondence between the gopis and Gaura's associates in verses 194–207 follows the order of the lists. The “Anubhashya” gives the verses as “195 and 202”; in our edition of the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” Bhagavatacharya is in verse 203 (202 is Jitamitra), and the “Anubhashya” on Adi 10.113 also gives verse 203. One of the biographies calls him Shveta-manjari without citing a primary source.
  9. In the “Narottama-vilasa” (8.57) a Bhagavata Acharya is also mentioned at a meal in the company of Achyutananda, Advaita's son. How many years passed between the Lord's pastimes and the Kheturi festival, and whether this is the same person, is not known.
